evidence: The change replaced the emailservice pod (new ReplicaSet scheduled, image pulled, started). Since then the new pod has kept failing its readiness and liveness probes, which time out connecting within 1s and are still recurring. The kubelet already killed and restarted the container once. The old pod was removed, so the service is now at 0 replicas, meaning nothing is serving. One of the 4 calls in the last 30s failed (25%). Latency seen by callers did not rise (p50 about 2.6 ms vs 3.1 ms), which argues against added network latency. The full pod replacement plus probe timeouts matches past emailservice incidents where a CPU limit was set to 125m or 150m. All of those ended at 0 replicas, repeated restarts and 100% errors, i.e. High severity. Confidence is lowered for three reasons: there were very few requests, it is only 30s in, and network-latency incidents look similar early on. No other service is measurably slower yet. Recommend rolling back the change.

So far emailservice looks healthy. Its latency hasn't changed: callers see p50 3.2→2.9 ms and its own spans 0.27 ms both before and after, with 0 errors. But that is only 4 requests in the last 30 s, so it's weak evidence. The warning sign is the new pod's startup: readiness checks failed 4 times (6–17 s) and liveness checks failed 2 times (10–15 s), each timing out at 1 s. It only became ready about 21 s in, when the old pod was stopped. There have been no restarts yet. At t=30 s, CPU jumped from about 4m to 64m and memory from 36 to 72 MiB, which looks like slow, CPU-starved startup. I can't confirm a CPU limit from this data; that's my best guess. Past emailservice incidents with this same early pattern (CPU limit set to 100–125m, or added network latency) all ended High: repeated liveness kills, restarts, and sometimes 0 replicas with 100% errors. No other service has been checked yet. It's too early to be sure because traffic is low and there are no restarts so far. I recommend rolling back, or at least watching closely for liveness kills and restarts.

The change replaced the paymentservice pod. The new pod was scheduled and started at about 3 s. Its readiness probe failed twice at 6–7 s, which is normal during startup, and the old pod was stopped at 16 s. Since then there is 1 replica with no restarts and no further warnings. Memory is steady at about 38 MiB, and the CPU jump to 59m at 30 s fits a pod that has just started. Paymentservice served very few requests, so its latency can't be compared reliably: 4 calls in the last 30 s against 1 in the baseline. Still, the median wait for callers is unchanged (4.0 to 4.0 ms), with 0% errors. Checkoutservice also served too few requests to compare reliably (4 vs 1, median about 28 ms), and none of the other services are significantly slower or returning more errors. The change itself is unknown. A past incident where the memory limit was set to 128Mi looked similar at 30 s but became High later, so I can't rule out a resource limit that only shows up over time. Confidence is moderate because there is little traffic and it is still early. Keep watching restarts, memory and checkout errors.

Since the change, nearly every adservice call fails: 98% errors over the last 30 s and 100% over the last 15 s. Callers see p50 latency of about 100.5 ms against a 1.47 ms baseline, which looks like the callers' 100 ms deadline cutting the calls off. There are no Kubernetes events, so the pod was not replaced and this is not a temporary handover between pods. The pod is still running (1 replica, 0 restarts) with flat CPU (~2m) and memory (91.7 MiB), so it looks healthy from the inside while calls to it time out. That points to added network delay rather than CPU, memory or the service being down. Frontend p50 has risen from 19.5 ms to 100 ms (+415%) as it waits for those timeouts. No other service is significantly slower. Past adservice incidents where 250–1000 ms of network latency was added looked the same at 30 s (high error rate, about 100 ms latency, frontend slower) and all ended High. Some of those pods later restarted or went to 0 replicas. Confidence is reduced because only 30 s of data exist and the change itself isn't known; latency and resource limits are inferred from symptoms.

Callers' view of adservice: 96% of calls fail, and nearly all hit what looks like a 100 ms client timeout (p50 100.6 ms vs a 1.46 ms baseline, p95 101 ms). That is far past the High threshold. adservice's CPU (about 2m) and memory (91.8 MiB) have not changed, there is still 1 replica with no restarts, and there are no Kubernetes events, so no pod was replaced. This is not the brief switch-over to a new pod, and it doesn't look like a CPU or memory limit. The pod itself looks healthy while calls to it time out, which points to delay added on the network. Frontend p50 rose from 18.6 to 115.7 ms because it waits out the ad timeout. All other services are unchanged. In past adservice incidents where 400-1000 ms of network latency was added, telemetry looked the same at 30 s; later, failed probes killed and restarted the pod, it ended at 0 replicas with 100% errors, and every case was rated High. The change has to be rolled back. It is only 30 s since the change and adservice has no traces of its own server-side timing to compare, so I can't fully rule out the service being unreachable rather than slow.

Callers now wait about 100 ms for adservice (p50 100.6 ms, p95 100.9 ms) against a baseline of 4.4 ms. The error rate is 95% over the last 30 s and 100% over the last 15 s. Almost every call stops at the same ~100 ms, which looks like the caller's timeout cutting off requests that would take longer. There are no Kubernetes events: no pod replacement, kills or probe failures. Replicas stay at 1, restarts stay at 3 (no new ones), and CPU (~11m) and memory (~79 MiB) are normal. So this is not the usual pod-swap blip, and nothing points to a CPU or memory limit. A delay added on the network path is the most likely cause, but I can't rule out adservice simply hanging, because no service-side span view was returned. Frontend p50 went from 21 ms to 116 ms because it waits out the ad timeout, though its error rate is still 0%. The problem is getting worse, not clearing, so I predict High severity and recommend rolling back the change.

The change scaled the emailservice deployment down to 0 replicas. The events show ReplicaSet emailservice-5b89f4dcb7 going from 1 to 0, the pod being deleted and no new pod being created. Metrics agree: replicas went from 1 to 0 and memory dropped from 35 MiB to 2.4 MiB. Since the change, emailservice has handled no requests itself, and the only call made to it in the last 30 s failed in 0.45 ms, which looks like a refused connection. That is just one call, so the error rate on its own is weak evidence; the strong evidence is the 0 replicas. No other service is slower or failing: checkoutservice's one recent request succeeded in about 26 ms, against a baseline of about 29 ms. This fits checkout carrying on when the order-confirmation email fails, though with so few checkouts I can't be sure. Confirmation emails won't be sent until emailservice is scaled back up, so roll back the change or restore the replicas.

Callers now wait about 503 ms for paymentservice (p50) compared with 2.4 ms at baseline, but paymentservice's own server spans have not slowed (0.21 ms vs 0.31 ms). The extra time is spent on the network, which points to injected network latency. The liveness probe has been failing on its 1 s connect timeout since t=2s, the kubelet killed the container at t=22s, and replicas dropped to 0 at t=30s. These are probe failures causing a restart, not the normal swap to a new pod, so the service is likely to keep restarting. Checkoutservice, which calls paymentservice, slowed from 25 ms to 521 ms p50. Its own spans and its callers' spans both show the slowdown. Frontend and all other services look unchanged. Latency is already far beyond double the baseline and the pod is restarting, so the final severity is High. Confidence is lowered because each window had very few payment requests (9 baseline, 3 recent) and only 30 s has passed.

The change scaled paymentservice's deployment down from 1 replica to 0. The events show the replica set scaled down and the only pod killed and deleted, and no replacement pod was scheduled. Metrics have shown 0 replicas since t=+15s. The one caller request since the change failed (error rate 100%, but that is a single request). The service handled no requests on its own side. With no pod left, checkoutservice's payment calls will keep failing. Only 3 requests reached paymentservice in the baseline, so the latency figures are weak evidence. The conclusion rests on the replica count and the events.

The change replaced the pod. The new productcatalogservice pod failed its readiness probe one second after starting ("failed to connect within 1s: context deadline exceeded"). The old pod was stopped at t=9s anyway. In the last 15s, callers got 100% errors on 25 requests, the new pod logged no server spans of its own, and failed calls returned in a median 0.09 ms, which looks like there was no ready pod to receive them. The slowest calls hung for about 15 s. Knock-on effects: frontend errors are at 84% over the last 15s (48% over 30s), checkoutservice failed its only 2 requests (too few to judge) and some recommendationservice calls hang for about 16 s. Memory fell to 5.8 MiB and CPU is down too. This doesn't look like the normal brief switchover: errors are rising, not clearing, about 20s after the old pod stopped, and the new pod never passed readiness. Past productcatalogservice incidents with this pattern (a new pod failing readiness on a 1s timeout, then 100% errors) came from added network latency and all ended High severity, with replicas at 0 and restarts. A scale-to-0 change is less likely because a new pod was created. The cause is inferred: network latency and plain unavailability look alike here, and it is only 30s since the change.

The change replaced the productcatalogservice pod. The new pod was scheduled and started at about 6–7 s. It failed one readiness probe at 8.4 s, which is normal right after startup, and the old pod was stopped at 9.4 s. Since then there are no further probe failures, no restarts and 1 replica. CPU (7–11 m) and memory (3–9 MiB) look normal. The service's own server spans are unchanged (p50 about 0.1 ms, 0 errors), so it is not processing slowly. What callers see looks like the changeover between pods: in the last 20 s, all 10 caller requests failed after hanging 17–19 s. That is close to the up-to-about-20 s hang expected while connections move from the old pod to the new one, and those calls started around when the old pod was stopped. Frontend shows the same knock-on effect (34% errors, p95 about 19 s) and traffic overall dropped for a while. recommendationservice is unaffected. None of this matches past bad changes to this service: added network latency and scale-to-zero cases all showed 0 replicas, restarts or repeated Unhealthy events, and none of those are present here. Confidence is low because it is too early to tell. The new pod has served no traffic yet that I can see, and the single request in the last 12 s failed fast (0.06 ms). Check again in 30–60 s: if callers' errors don't clear once the new pod is serving, roll the change back.

The change caused a normal rollout. The new frontend pod was scheduled and started at 2.8–3.8 s, and the old pod was stopped at 14.8 s. There are no restarts, no Unhealthy events, replicas stay at 1 and the error rate is 0%. Median latency hasn't moved (17.2 ms vs 17.2 ms baseline), so this doesn't look like added network latency: past frontend latency injections pushed the median up by thousands of percent. Tail latency is up, though: p95 went from 26.9 ms to 109 ms over the last 30 s and is still 87 ms over the last 12 s, after the old pod had been stopped. That points to something lasting, not just the pod handover. The test doesn't call it significant yet (p=0.13–0.32). CPU is unchanged at about 20m, and memory dropped to 5 MiB because the pod is new. A higher tail with an unchanged median fits CPU throttling from a new, tighter CPU limit. A similar past case (EXP_0231, frontend CPU limit set to 100m) ended at Medium. Past memory-limit changes to frontend ended at Low, so a memory limit is the other possibility. No other service is measurably slower. It's only 30 s in, so confidence is low: keep watching frontend p95, and roll back or raise the CPU limit if the tail stays high.

The change replaced the shippingservice pod. The new pod was scheduled at about 5 s and started at 6 s. It failed one readiness probe at 7 s, and the old pod was stopped at the same moment. There have been no restarts or repeated probe failures since, replicas stay at 1, and CPU (about 1 mcore) and memory (3 MiB on the fresh pod) look normal. Over the last 30 s, callers saw a median latency of 1.21 ms against a 1.03 ms baseline, which is not a significant slowdown. However, 41% of calls failed and p95 was about 19.6 s, which matches the roughly 20 s hang-or-fail pattern of callers switching from the old pod to the new one. The last 10–15 s still look bad, but on very few calls: 4–5 requests with a median of 2–4 s and 50–60% errors. Those calls may have started during the switchover. The one checkout in the last 15 s, which calls shippingservice, finished normally in 27 ms. The only other service showing errors is frontend, and those come from its shipping calls. In past incidents where network latency was added to shippingservice, the pod kept restarting and replicas dropped to 0. None of that is happening here. Confidence is limited because it is early and the recent sample is tiny. Keep watching: if latency stays in the seconds or errors stay high once the switchover is over, roll back.

The change has rolled out a new adservice pod (adservice-5dbb89c7d7-s9vt7). It was scheduled at 2.8 s and the container started at 9.8 s. There is no Killing event yet, so the old pod is probably still serving traffic, and it is too early to see how the new pod behaves under load. Latency as callers see it hasn't changed: p50 is 1.23 ms against 1.29 ms at baseline, p95 is 2.37 ms against 1.93 ms, there are 0% errors (41 requests in the last 30 s), and the change is not statistically significant. No other service is measurably slower, and there are no restarts, Unhealthy events or replica loss. CPU went from about 2m to 95.6m and memory from 94 to 154 MiB, which fits a Java (JVM) pod starting up. Past adservice incidents with this same early pattern ended both ways. Under normal traffic, a 200Mi memory limit and a 250m CPU limit both ended Low. Under high traffic, a 200m CPU limit ended High, with latency up 269% by 170 s. Traffic is normal now, so I lean Low, but a tight CPU limit can't be ruled out until the new pod is taking traffic. Recheck latency and the Unhealthy/Killing events in 1–2 minutes.

The change replaced the adservice pod. A new pod (adservice-6dbbc49859-r9wxj) was scheduled at 2.9 s and started at 3.9 s. It has no restarts, there are no Unhealthy or Killing events, and the deployment still has 1 replica. The old pod has not been stopped yet, so callers are probably still being served by it, which makes this an early read. Callers see adservice latency as unchanged or slightly better: p50 3.26 ms vs 3.88 ms baseline (p95 5.33 vs 6.77 ms), with 0% errors. No other service is measurably slower. In the last sample, CPU rose from about 13m to 96m and memory from about 82 MiB to 130 MiB. That fits a Java service starting up alongside the old pod, rather than an injected fault. Past incidents with the same early pattern (pod replaced at normal traffic, latency flat) mostly ended Low: a 250m CPU limit and a 200Mi memory limit. The exception was a 200m CPU limit under high traffic, which was already restarting at 30 s and ended High. Network-latency incidents showed large latency increases and errors within 30 s, which we don't see. I can't yet rule out a tight CPU or memory limit hurting the new pod once it takes traffic, so watch its CPU, memory, restarts and caller latency over the next 2–3 minutes.

The change replaced the recommendationservice pod. The new pod (x6vpm) failed its readiness probe 3 times and its liveness probe twice: it could not accept a connection within 1 s. The old pod was stopped at about 15 s. In the last 10 s, callers saw 100% errors on 22 requests, failing almost instantly (p50 0.04 ms), and the service recorded no requests of its own. That means no working pod is serving traffic. Over the last 30 s the caller error rate is 33%, up from 0%. Repeated liveness failures usually lead to restarts. There are none yet, so the restart part is a prediction. Requests that did get through earlier were not slower (p50 about 4 ms, same as baseline), so added network latency is unlikely. Past incidents with added latency showed latency up by 200x or more. CPU jumped to 46m (normal is about 12m), and the probes timed out while the container was starting. This fits a tight CPU limit, like past incident EXP_0297 (CPU limit set to 100m), which ended High with repeated restarts. The cause is not certain, but the outcome looks High either way. No other service is measurably slower or failing yet; the frontend shows no errors, so it may be handling the failed recommendation calls. Recommend rolling back the change.

The change rolled out a new adservice pod: ReplicaSet adservice-98d766b7 was scaled up and its pod was scheduled and started about 4 s after the change, using the same image (v0.10.5). This looks like a resource-limit or config change rather than a code change. The old pod has not been stopped yet, so the new pod may not be serving most traffic, and it is too early to judge the final state. What callers see is unchanged so far: p50 1.29 ms vs 1.27 ms baseline, p95 2.35 ms vs 2.46 ms, 0% errors, not statistically different (39 requests in the last 30 s). There are no restarts, no probe failures and 1 replica. The 30 s metric sample shows CPU jumping from about 2m to 88.6m and memory from 93 to 159 MiB, which fits Java startup on the new pod. Similar past adservice rollouts with this early pattern (CPU limit 250m, memory limit 180Mi, normal traffic) ended Low. One with a CPU limit of 200m ended Medium. One under high traffic with a 200m CPU limit had restarted 6 times by 30 s and ended High. Without seeing the new pod handle steady traffic, I can't rule out a tight CPU or memory limit. Keep watching latency, restarts and OOM/Unhealthy events for the next few minutes.

The change scaled the cartservice deployment from 1 replica to 0. Events show the old pod being stopped and the replica set deleted, with no new pod scheduled. Metrics show replicas dropping from 1 to 0 at about t=15s. Over the last 30s, 100% of calls failed (31 requests): most failed straight away (p50 0.07ms) and some hung (p95 about 19s). In the 60s baseline there were no errors and p50 was 1.4ms. This is not a normal pod swap, because nothing replaces the old pod. Frontend and checkoutservice are listed because they call cartservice and will lose cart functions. I did not check the service map or their latency to confirm this. Rolling back the change, or scaling cartservice back to 1 replica, should fix it.

Only one checkout request completed in the last 30 s. It took about 1.24 s as frontend saw it and 1.14 s in checkoutservice's own server span, against a baseline of about 19 ms (3 requests). The added time is in checkoutservice's calls to other services, not in those services. Checkout's calls to emailservice took about 108 ms, while emailservice's own span was 0.92 ms. Its calls to paymentservice took about 104 ms, while paymentservice's own span was 0.53 ms. In baseline these calls took about 3 ms. About 100 ms added to each of roughly 10 calls matches the 1.1 s total. That points to network delay added on checkoutservice's traffic. CPU is flat at about 1 millicore and memory at about 8 MiB. There are no events (no pod replacement, no restarts), the single replica is up, and there are no errors. Other services' own latency is unchanged, except that frontend waits longer for checkout. The cause is not a pod switchover, because no new pod was started, so the delay should persist. Latency over 2x baseline means High severity. Confidence is moderate because the evidence is a single request.

Frontend's median latency went from 15.75 ms to 5117 ms (about 325 times its baseline), with 0% errors so far. Every call frontend makes to another service now takes about 500 ms longer than before (currency, productcatalog, recommendation and checkout, each measured from frontend's side). Those services' own request times have not changed, so the delay is in frontend's network path rather than in their processing. That fits about 500 ms of network delay added to frontend's traffic. The kubelet's liveness and readiness health checks on frontend's /_healthz endpoint are timing out, and at about 28 s the container was killed and is being restarted. There was no rollout and no new pod; the same pod is failing its health checks. Frontend's CPU fell from about 19.5m to 12.6m, which looks like it is sitting idle waiting on the network rather than being throttled by a CPU limit. Past incidents with 200–1000 ms of latency added to frontend showed the same pattern: repeated restarts, sometimes ending with no pods serving, and all were rated High. The other services look healthy from their own side, but they are only slower as frontend sees them, so the user-facing damage is all through frontend. Recommend rolling back the change now.

About 1 s of network delay appears to have been added to the frontend pod. Its p50 latency went from 15 ms to about 10,100 ms (p95 about 13,500 ms). Every outgoing call from frontend now takes about 1,000 ms as frontend sees it: currencyservice, productcatalogservice and recommendationservice all show this. Yet those services' own spans are unchanged (sub-ms to about 2 ms), so they are processing normally and the delay is on frontend's network path. There were no events for a new pod being scheduled, so this is not a normal pod swap. The liveness probe on /_healthz is timing out, the restart count rose from 4 to 5, and replicas dropped to 0 in the latest sample. Past incident EXP_0293 (1000 ms network latency added to frontend) looked the same and ended High, with repeated restarts and no requests served. The slower downstream services are only slow in frontend's view, so frontend is the only affected service. Checkout, cart, payment, shipping and email had no calls to compare in the last 30 s. Recommend rolling back the change.

Callers now wait a steady ~200 ms on productcatalogservice (p50 200.8 ms, p95 202.0 ms, 308 requests) against a 0.6 ms baseline. Its own server spans have barely changed (0.09 to 0.11 ms), so the time is being added on the network, not in processing. There are no pod events (no replacement or restarts), so this is not a rollout blip. CPU (~8.5 mc) and memory (~11 MiB) are flat, and errors are 0%. The delay is spreading upstream: recommendationservice p50 went from 2 to 202 ms and frontend p50 from 16 to 1417 ms, because the frontend makes several catalog calls per page. Checkout went from 18 to 1029 ms, but that is a single request so it is only a weak signal. Latency is far more than double the baseline, which makes this High. Roll back the change.

Early read, low confidence. The change replaced the checkoutservice pod: a new pod was scheduled at about 3.4 s, started at 4.4 s, and the old pod was stopped at 5.4 s. The new pod failed one readiness probe right after starting, which is normal during startup. No restarts so far and replicas=1. Callers saw 6 of 7 calls fail (86%) with p50 around 8 s in the last 30 s, and all 3 calls failed in the last 10 s (p50 around 5 s). Those slow failures match calls left hanging during the pod swap. The one request that reached the new pod (checkoutservice's own spans) succeeded in 27.9 ms against a 25.7 ms baseline, so the new pod seems to handle work normally. Checkout traffic is tiny (3 requests in the baseline), so this proves little. CPU (2.3m) and memory (3.6 MiB) are small, as expected for a fresh pod. No other service is slower. Frontend errors rose to 8.1% (6 s p95), which fits failed checkout calls. Past checkoutservice changes that replaced the pod, such as CPU or memory limit changes, looked like this at 30 s and ended Low. The changes that ended High showed 0 replicas or repeated restarts, which I don't see here. Risk: errors were still at 100% in the last 10 s, about 25 s after the swap, slightly past the usual transition time. Watch over the next minute. If checkout errors or multi-second latency continue once the new pod is serving traffic, or the pod starts restarting, roll back the change.

Checkoutservice handled only one request in the last 30 s, so this rests on thin data. That request took 723 ms as frontend saw it and 673 ms in checkoutservice's own spans, against a p50 of about 24 ms before the change, roughly 28 times slower. Inside that request, checkoutservice's outgoing calls to paymentservice and emailservice each took about 53 ms, up from 2–3 ms. Those services' own spans show they worked as fast as before (0.3 ms), so about 50 ms is being added on the network around checkoutservice. A checkout makes many downstream calls, so this adds up to hundreds of ms. CPU is still about 1.5 millicores, memory is flat at 8.2 MiB, and there are no Kubernetes events: no pod replacement, restarts or kills. That rules out a resource limit, a crash, or the brief slowdown while a new pod takes over, so the delay is probably the lasting state. All other services' own latency is unchanged and nothing shows errors. Frontend's overall latency is unchanged, but its checkout requests will be slow. This points to added network delay on checkoutservice, which would be High severity (latency more than double baseline). I recommend rolling back the change. Confidence is moderate because of the single sample.

The change replaced currencyservice's pod. The new pod was scheduled at about 3.6 s and started at 5.6 s. Its readiness probe then timed out 4 times (6.6 to 18.6 s) and its liveness probe 2 times (15.6 and 25.6 s), each failing to connect within 1 s. The old pod was stopped at 27.6 s. The new pod is using much more CPU and memory: about 57m CPU against a 13m baseline (+300%) and 85 MiB against 50 MiB. There are no restarts yet and still 1 replica. Latency as callers see it is about the same as before: p50 is 1.70 ms against 1.65 ms, with 0 errors, and nothing is significantly slower. But most of those calls were probably served by the old pod, which was only stopped about 2 s before the data ends. This pattern (CPU jump, memory up about 80%, probe failures while the pod starts) closely matches past changes that lowered the CPU limit (100m to 150m). Those ended anywhere from Low to High, and the lower the limit, the worse the outcome. Calls to the new pod in the last 10 s look normal so far: p50 1.74 ms, p95 2.86 ms, 0 errors, and the service's own processing time is up about 14% but not significantly. Nothing has degraded yet, so I recommend monitoring rather than rolling back. Watch the next 1–2 minutes for a third liveness failure or restarts, and for rising latency or errors. If either appears, raise the CPU limit or roll back. My confidence is low because it is too early to see how the new pod behaves under full traffic.

The change rolled out a new emailservice pod (new ReplicaSet, Scheduled/Created/Started events). Within seconds of starting, that pod failed both its readiness and liveness probes, which time out connecting to port 8080 within 1s. Kubernetes then killed the container for failing liveness, and the restart count went from 7 to 8. While it was starting, CPU jumped from about 3m to 48m and memory from 36 to 56 MiB. That looks like a CPU-starved slow startup. It matches past incident EXP_0354 (emailservice CPU limit set to 100m), which kept restarting and ended High. The past network-latency cases looked different: replicas dropped to 0 and no new pod was rolled out. The restart loop alone puts this at High severity. Latency can't be judged: emailservice served only 1 request in the last 30s (10 in the baseline). No other service was checked, so I've listed only emailservice as affected. Confidence is moderate because it's only 30s in and the cause is inferred from one past incident.

The change replaced the recommendationservice pod. The new pod started at about 5 s and failed its liveness probe twice and its readiness probe three times between 10 and 17 s. That fits a normal startup, because the pod then passed readiness and the old pod was stopped at 22 s. There have been no restarts and there is still 1 replica. Measured by callers, median latency is 4.15 ms against a 4.27 ms baseline over the last 30 s, and 4.48 ms over the last 10 s, which is not significantly slower. The service's own timings are also unchanged, and there are no errors across 59 requests. No other service is significantly slower or failing. CPU rose to about 71 millicores and memory to about 70 MiB, roughly double the old pod's figures, which looks like the new pod warming up. This closely matches past incident EXP_0324 (memory limit set to 220Mi), which showed the same probe failures and CPU and memory jump at 30 s and ended Low. It also resembles past incidents where a tight CPU limit (100–150m) caused probe failures at startup and later restart loops. Those ended High, so I can't rule that out yet. I'm not more confident because it is only 30 s after the change and the new pod has served traffic for about 8 s. Keep monitoring for more failed health checks, restarts, or CPU levelling off flat near a limit over the next 2–3 minutes.

Checkoutservice's median latency went from about 20 ms to 445 ms as the frontend sees it, and from 19.7 ms to 409 ms in its own spans. That is over 20 times slower, with no errors so far. The services it calls are not slower in their own spans: payment is 0.3 ms and email 0.3 ms, both unchanged. But checkoutservice's calls to them each take about 38 ms longer (payment 2.8 to 38.5 ms, email 3.1 to 38.1 ms), and the frontend sees about 36 ms more on top of checkoutservice's own time. A roughly fixed delay added to every network call into and out of checkoutservice points to network latency. A checkout makes many calls one after another, so the delays add up. There are no Kubernetes events (no pod was replaced or restarted). CPU stays around 1.5 millicores and memory around 8 MiB, so this is not a CPU or memory limit, and it is not a passing pod switchover. Other services' medians are unchanged; the frontend's p95 rose from 33 to 82 ms, probably because of slow checkout requests. I expect latency to stay above double the baseline, which makes the final severity High. Confidence is lowered because checkoutservice handled only 3 requests in the last 30 s (7 in the baseline), but the result was still significant (p = 0.008).

Frontend's own p50 latency went from 17.6 ms to 405 ms (p95 from 35 to 660 ms, p=1e-23), more than 20 times its baseline, with no errors. Every outgoing call from frontend now takes about 35 ms longer: currencyservice is 1.6→36.8 ms, productcatalogservice 0.8→36 ms and recommendationservice 4.3→39 ms as frontend sees them. Those services' own server spans are basically unchanged. So the delay is on frontend's network path, not in the services it calls, and it adds up across the many calls each page makes. There are no Kubernetes events for frontend: no new pod was started and nothing restarted, so this is not the usual pod-replacement blip that clears within a minute. CPU (about 20 millicores) and memory (about 15 MiB) are flat, which rules out CPU or memory limits. This looks like added network delay that will last, keeping frontend latency well above double its baseline, so severity is High and the change should be rolled back. Confidence is 0.85 rather than higher because only 30 seconds of data exist so far. Lower-traffic services (cart, checkout, email, payment, shipping) got no requests in the last 30 s, so their status can't be checked yet.

The rollout created a new currencyservice pod (6dfcd9c668-cw7bt). From t=5 s to t=26 s that pod failed its readiness probe 4 times and its liveness probe 2 times, each time with 'failed to connect within 1s', so 26 s after starting it is still not ready. One more liveness failure should make Kubernetes restart it, which would start a restart loop. CPU jumped from about 29m to 69m and memory from about 54 to 76 MiB at the last sample (t=30 s), which looks like a slow, CPU-throttled startup. Past currencyservice incidents with the same pattern (startup CPU and memory spike plus Unhealthy probe events) were CPU limit changes. Those with limits of 100m and 125m ended High, 140m ended Medium and 150m ended Low. Here the probes are failing more often than in those incidents, so I lean towards High. Callers don't see a problem yet: the old pod is still serving, error rate is 0%, p50 latency is only about 10% higher, and no other service is significantly slower, so there is no downstream impact so far. Confidence is moderate because it is only 30 s after the change and the new pod has not taken traffic yet. I recommend rolling back the change, or raising the CPU limit instead.

The rollout looks normal. A new paymentservice pod was scheduled and started, failed its readiness probe twice during startup, and then took over. The old pod was stopped at 15.8 s. There is 1 replica and no restarts. Memory is steady at about 38–42 MiB. CPU jumped to 55m at t=30 s, which looks like the new pod starting up, as in past rollouts that changed only the CPU limit and ended Low. Caller-observed latency went from a p50 of 2.95 ms to 4.0 ms, with 0% errors. That change is not significant (p=0.09) and rests on only 3 requests. The pod's own server-side timings are also unchanged. No other service is significantly slower or failing, and checkoutservice's apparent slowdown is also based on only 3 requests and not significant. There is no sign of added network latency (past cases showed a p50 near 150–1000 ms), of the service going down, or of memory pressure. Confidence is limited because traffic is very low and it is only 30 s after the change, so keep watching CPU and restarts.

The change swapped productcatalogservice's pod in the usual way. The new pod was scheduled, pulled, created and started at t≈4.7s. It failed one readiness probe at 5.7s, a common startup blip. The old pod was stopped at 5.7s. Replicas stayed at 1 with 0 restarts. The new pod's CPU (~15m) and memory (5.8 MiB) look like a healthy fresh process with no sign of limit pressure. Over the 30s window the service's own spans are unchanged (p50 0.09 ms vs 0.09 ms baseline, 0 errors). Callers saw 4.5% errors and a p95 of 10 ms, and frontend saw 20% errors and a p95 of about 17.6s. Those errors come from calls hanging 11–19s around the switchover, which matches the normal transition stall rather than a lasting fault. A past incident with the same rollout events (EXP_0250, memory limit set to 64Mi) also showed errors at 30s and ended Low. In the past network-latency and scale-to-0 incidents, replicas showed 0 and pods restarted, and none of that is happening here. Main caveat: in the last 20s, all 10 caller requests failed and the service recorded no server spans, so it is not yet confirmed that the new pod is serving traffic. Confidence is lowered for that reason. If the errors are still there after about 60s, roll back the change.

The change scaled the shippingservice deployment down to 0 replicas at t+0.6s. The old pod was stopped and no new pod was scheduled, and the replica count in metrics has stayed at 0 since t+15s. So this is not a normal pod swap: nothing is left to serve requests. In the last 30s, callers of shippingservice saw 85% errors, with p50 latency of 6.3s and p95 of 19.6s against a baseline of 0.9ms and 2ms. The failure is spreading upstream: checkoutservice errors are at 75% (only 4 requests, so that figure is rough), and frontend errors are at 22% with p95 latency of 17s. All other services look normal. Roll back the change to restore the replica.

Over the 30 s since the change, about 95% of calls to adservice failed (baseline 0%, 115 requests, so the error rate is reliable). Callers waited about 100 ms per call (p50 100.5 ms against a 1.2 ms baseline), which looks like callers giving up at a timeout rather than the service being slow. The liveness and readiness probes have kept failing since about 5 s after the change ('failed to connect within 1s'), and liveness failures will likely trigger restarts. CPU stays near idle (about 4 millicores) and memory is flat at 95.6 MiB, which rules out CPU or memory limits. Adservice is not accepting connections, so I classed it as unavailable; blocked network traffic can't be fully ruled out. Frontend p50 rose from 16.5 to 114.5 ms because it waits for adservice to time out, but frontend itself shows no errors.

Callers now wait about 500 ms for emailservice (p50 was 2.4 ms) and 33% of calls fail. Emailservice's own server spans are unchanged (about 0.3 ms), which points to added network delay rather than slow processing. The liveness probe keeps failing and Kubernetes keeps killing the pod: at 30 s there were 0 replicas, 1 restart, and memory had fallen from 36.6 to 2.7 MiB. Checkoutservice also slowed, from 18 ms to 515 ms p50 (significant at p=0.0085 as its callers see it), so the frontend's checkout path will be slower too (I didn't check frontend directly). Three similar past emailservice incidents with 400–1000 ms of added network latency all became restart loops with 100% errors (High). Sample sizes are small (6 requests in the last 30 s), so confidence is moderate.

Thirty seconds after the change, productcatalogservice is badly degraded, and the most likely cause is about 1 s of added network delay in front of it. Callers now wait a median of about 1001 ms (baseline 0.68 ms) and 12.5% of their calls fail. The service's own processing time is almost unchanged at 0.11 ms (baseline 0.09 ms), so the delay is between callers and the service, not inside it. Its health check has a 1 s timeout, so the check keeps failing from about 2 s after the change. Kubernetes killed and restarted the container at about 22 s, and replicas are now 0 with 1 restart. These events are still recurring, so it should keep failing checks and restarting while the change is in place. This is not the normal short handover between pods: there is no new pod being scheduled, only the existing pod failing and being killed. Knock-on effects: frontend median rose from 16 ms to 1011 ms with 32% errors, and recommendationservice from 2 ms to about 1002 ms. The one checkout request in the window failed, but that is a single request so it is weak evidence. Confidence is reduced because only 30 s of data exist since the change. Roll back the change.

Callers now wait about 202 ms for emailservice, up from about 2.6 ms before the change. emailservice's own server spans have barely moved (0.26 to 0.33 ms), so the extra time is in the network, not in processing. There are no pod events: no new pod, no restarts. CPU, memory and replicas are flat, so this is not a pod handover and not resource pressure. Latency is far more than double the baseline, which makes this High. The sample is very small, though (2 to 3 requests in each window), so the result is not statistically confirmed and confidence is lower.

No new pod was scheduled. Instead the existing emailservice pod failed its liveness probe (it could not connect within 1s), so Kubernetes killed and restarted it: restarts went from 6 to 7 and replicas are now 0. Callers now wait p50 450 ms and p95 855 ms, against a 2.6 ms baseline, and every recent call failed (100% errors), while the service's own server spans show no requests. CPU was flat at about 3m before the restart, which makes a CPU limit unlikely. The pattern matches past emailservice incidents where 400-450 ms of network latency was added: liveness timeouts and Killing events with no rescheduling, about 450 ms seen by callers, ending in repeated restarts and 100% errors (High). checkoutservice is also slower (p50 18 ms to 465 ms) because it waits on email calls. Only 2 requests came in during the window, so the evidence is thin and confidence is moderate.
